item.title: The Analytic Signal
item.description: This post focuses on the analytic signal. The analytic-signal view is central in communications, radar, controls, and physics-based signal analysis because it separates amplitude and phase behavior in a mathematically clean way. The word “analytic” here is not a coincidence of terminology — it’s the same complex-analysis concept from a math methods course, applied on the time axis instead of the spatial or complex-variable axis it’s usually introduced with. This post builds the signal-processing machinery first, then closes the loop back to complex analysis to show why the name fits.

item.title: Quantum RF Sensing
item.description: In this post I work through the question: can a quantum RF receiver replace my traditional receiver? I had a perfect excuse to answer it. I was building a downlink for the GOES-R geosynchronous weather satellite, and the link budget was tight enough to make any noise-floor improvement worth chasing. So I looked hard at Rydberg-atom receivers, did the math, and came away with a nuanced answer. This post walks you through what I found, with equations, scaling laws, and a couple of scripts you can run yourself.

item.title: Collecting L-band Satellite Signals
item.description: In the past, I have captured signals at 137.1 MHz from the NOAA 19 weather satellite using a discone antenna without any pointing. It was exciting to see weather images appear on the computer monitor after processing the signals. At the time, I planned to find a way to set up a tracking capability so I could track the satellites while pointing a higher gain antenna at them to get better signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and longer collection time. Well, I have finally put together a system that can do this for L-band and UHF frequencies. A system adequate for x-band is in the works.

item.title: Parabolic Dish Antenna Basics
item.description: If you plan to dive into a Radio Frequency (RF) project, getting familiar with a few core antenna types is essential. Choosing or designing the right antenna is one of the most fundamental skills in electrical engineering, and understanding the first principles behind them will help you move quickly from concept to a working system that transmits and receives reliably.

item.title: From Vision to Prototype
item.description:
This post describes my teaching and mentoring approach that has evolved over the past decade through mentoring new engineering hires and summer interns. The approach emphasizes system-level thinking, project-driven learning, and just-in-time introduction of theoretical principles, with the aim of bridging the gap between classroom instruction and the realities of engineering practice.

The method unfolds in four stages: establishing a vision, decomposing into subsystems, cycling between systems and principles, and validating through demonstration.

item.title: Observing Satellites
item.description:
Observing satellites in the night sky can be a fun way to learn about orbital dynamics and learn your way around the earth and sky. This discussion is specific to observers in the northern hemisphere since I am currently living in the Rocky Mountain West area.

First, let’s review some important terminology:

Azimuth is the horizontal angle, measured in degrees, from true north in a clockwise direction. The star Polaris lies within one degree of true north and is therefore a useful reference point for determining azimuth in the night sky. To locate Polaris, first find the Big Dipper (Ursa Major) and identify the two stars that form the far edge of the dipper’s cup. Extending an imaginary line through these stars about five times their spacing will point to Polaris, a magnitude~+2 star. Because of the geometry of Earth’s rotation, Polaris appears at an altitude approximately equal to the observer’s latitude.

item.title: Startup Lessons Learned
item.description:
This post curates my lessons learned while building and running a small tech startup from 2014 to 2022. During that time, I kept a journal of the most important lessons I learned from starting and serving as CEO of KickView Corporation for 8 years. It was, without question, a challenging and rewarding period of my career. Hopefully, others can benefit from the lessons I learned along the way.

The most important lesson

One of the best things about doing a startup is the people - the ones you work with and the ones you meet along the way. I would say the experience helped me connect with people in ways that were not possible while I was an engineer at an established company. When you are the founder of a startup, you quickly learn the value of a wide variety of skills needed for running a business - accounting, legal services, commercial real estate, janitorial services, construction and building maintenance, administration, marketing, business development, etc. There are so many talents and skills needed to make the business world function, and engineering is only one small piece of that apparatus. It was humbling (in a good way) to meet so many talented and hard-working people adding value through their various skills and domain expertise. So, my first lesson learned (and most important) is to stay humble, appreciate and respect other people, and embrace the opportunity to interact with and learn from others.

item.title: My Reading Recommendations
item.description:
This is a list of reading suggestions based on what I have found educational and enjoyable. I will continue to update the list as I discover more books worth sharing information about. Warning: I primarily like to read non-fiction.

1. Seven Brief Lessons on Physics, by Carlo Rovelli
This is a well-written book that is both educational and enjoyable. It is a short book, so it can be read in a weekend. I highly recommend it for anyone interested in modern physics.

item.title: Deep Learning with Radio Frequency Signals
item.description: Signal Classification Using Spectrograms and Deep Learning In this post, I will introduce some basic methods for utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to process spectrograms created from Radio Frequency (RF) data. The information in the post was taken from a tutorial my colleagues and I provided to NVidia Corporation in early 2015 that has been used in their enterprise training series for several years. This post links you to a git project that removes the dependency on Nvidia’s DIGITS platform and uses only Keras and Tensorflow. Project Code & Data
